Question: What happened during the (SGCW) Battle of Fondor in Star Wars Legends?
Answer: The Battle of Fondor was one of the most important clashes of the Second Galactic Civil War, and it’s impacts were felt for decades to come. But in order to understand what happened and why it was so it important, we need to understand the battle’s backstory. Following the devestating Yuuzhan Vong War, the New Republic was reformed into the Galactic Alliance. However, tensions in the Alliance began to erupt over increased Corellian independance, and a war broke out between the Alliance and an increasing number of rebellious systems known as the Confederation, lead by Corellia. Han and Leia’s son, Jacen Solo, had fallen to the Dark Side and taken the moniker Darth Caedus, and the Mon Calamari Admiral Cha Nithal formed an alliance. They were able to launch a sucessful a coup to take over the Galctic Alliance. The two became Joint Chiefs of State, and lead the war effort against the Confederation. Cha Nithal Increasingly disgusted by the actions of the Galactic Alliance, which under the leadership of Jacen Solo had become increasingly totalitarian, the Jedi and Hapans withdrew from the war. This lead to a series of bloody clashes between the Galactic Alliance, Jedi and Hapan forces, and the Confederation at Kashyyyk, Balmorra, Kuat, and Centerpoint. The Anakin Solo fires on milenium old Wroshyyr forests during the Battle of Kashyyyk With both sides’ forces being worn down, the Confederation and Galactic Alliance were in search of new allies. Jacen Solo set his Sith apprentice, Tahiri Veila to Bastion, where he found an ally in Gilead Paelleon, the leader of the Imperial Remnant. They promised Paeelon the planets Bilbringi and Borelias in exchange for the Remnant’s support. Meanwhile, the Confederation found the support of the major shipbuilding world of Fondor. Realizing the importance of taking Fondor, Jacen Solo sent half of the Galactic Alliance fourth fleet to Fondor. Tahiri Veila also convinced Gilead Paelleon to send forces from the Imperial Remnant to help the Galactic Alliance. Gilead Paelleon Jacen Solo, Cha Nithal, and the Imperial Remnant arrived over Fondor, pushing throuigh the Confederation fleet before beginning to orbitally bombard the planet. Fondor surrendered, but Jacen Solo believed that Fondor hadn’t been punished enough. He refused to accept Fondor’s surrender, continuing to orbitally bombard Fondor’s cities, killing millions. Disgusted at Jacen’s actions, Cha Nihal attempted to relieve Solo of his command- but this backfired when two-thirds of the Alliance fleet joined Solo and began to engage Nithal’s forces. Gilead Paelleon, however, was equally disgusted with Jacen’s actions as Nithal, and so ordered his forces to join that of Nithal’s. This was in vain, however, as Paelleon was killed by Tahiri Veila, and the Imperial Remnant elected to join Solo. Tahiri Veila As Paelleon lay dying, the battle began heavily turning against Nithal, as she was badly outnumbered. However, Paelleon commed his old friend Natasi Daala, who had been building up her forces in the Maw Installation for decades. Daala, who’s forces were equipped with Metal-Crystal Phase Shifters, joined the battle on Nithal’s side. Natasi Daala The suprise of Daala’s entry into the battle (Daala was thought dead at the Battle of Columus over 20 years ago) and her Metal-Crystal Phase Shifters (which could pentrate shields) were able to turn the battle against Caedus. He was forced to retreat, though Nithal’s forces had taken heavy casualties. Jacen Solo during the battle Ultimately, however, the battle furthered Caedus’ plans. Though Caedus had been forced to retreat from the battlefield, he was now in complete control of the Galactic Alliance, and had the loyalty of the Imperial Remnant. This would lead to Caedus’ push against the Jedi and Hapan coalition, and lead to the fateful Battle of Shedu Maad, where the fate of the war would be decided. So, that is what happened at the Battle of Fondor, and why it was so important. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: Can socialism actually work within a capitalist economy?
Answer: No. Socialism is defined as worker control over the means of production, the abolition class, and the distribution of goods to meet human needs rather than profit. Capitalism is defined as private ownership of the means of production, and is characterized by a strict, hierarchical class division between the working class and the ruling class. The profit motive is all consuming. As you can see, these economic situations are not compatible. You cannot have a dictatorship of the proletariat, in which the sole class and ruling class is the working class, and the class divisions of capitalism. You cannot both manufacture goods to meet human needs and profit, because profit incentives rarely align with human needs. And you cannot have the average workers control the means of production while having a tiny minority of people control the means of production at once. Capitalism and socialism are not mutually compatible. One common misconception about socialism is that “socialism is when the government does stuff.” That is incorrect, as government intervention in the economy can occur in capitalist countries. Social democracies, such as those found in the Nordic Countries, are capitalist with a strong social safety net. In conclusion, socialism cannot work in a capitalist economy. In order to achieve a better world, we must immediately dismantle capitalism and achieve worker control of the means of production. We must kill capitalism before it kills us. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: What Star Wars battle was really important but is almost never talked about?
Answer: In Legends, the Second Battle of Obroa-Skai. Unless you’re a really big Star Wars EU fan, you’ve probably never heard of the Second Battle of Obroa-Skai. Essentially, it took place during the Yuuzhan Vong War shortly after Operation Emperor’s Spear and the Fall of Coruscant. The Second Battle of Obroa-Skai was a really important battle, however, it only gets a footnote in Galactic History. This battle saw X-Wings under Rogue Squadron and Kyp’s Dozen, along with capital ships under Keyan Farlander, as well as Hapan forces under Tenel Ka, destroy a large Vong fleet under commander Komm Krash. This battle was important for four reasons. First off, it saw the first use of Yammosk Jammers. The extra-galactic invaders the Yuuzhan Vong employed war coordinators, called jammers. The New Republic had created a Yammosk Jammer to stop the Yammosk’s ability to coordinate Yuuzhan Vong fleets, however, it had become ineffective. The New Republic realized they were using a second Yammosk and so employed a second Yammosk Jammer for the first time, which was crucial in their victory. Yammosks like the one above coordinated the Vong effort, and allowed Vong ships to have a level of coordination similar to that granted by battle melds. Second off, the fleet under Komm Krash was the last Yuuzhan Vong extra-galactic reserve fleet. By destroying it, the Vong could expect no further reinforcements- which seriously hurt Yuuzhan Vong morale. Thirdly, it helped New Republic morale immensely. Obroa-Skai was a world of cultural significance to the New Republic, as it held the largest libraries in the galaxy. By retaking it, the New Republic not only showed that the Vong weren’t unbeatable but they also reclaimed an important planet. Finally, this was the first time Hapans and the New Republic had worked together since the disastrous Battle of Fondor. This combined victory helped build respect and trust between the two allies- something that would be needed for the upcoming Battle of Coruscant. Above: The Hapan Navy In conclusion, the Second Battle of Obroa-Skai was one of the most important battles of the Yuuzhan Vong War- but it is rarely mentioned. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: Did colonialism benefit or harm Africa?
Answer: Colonialism hurt Africa. The pernicious myth that colonialism helped Africa has become increasingly widespread lately. This fiction- the modern-day version of “white man's burden” purports that colonialism helped Africa because the European powers built infrastructure and brought modern technology to Africa. However, Africa was not a barbaric land devoid of technology before the European’s arrival, but rather an incredibly diverse continent full of advanced civilizations. In parts of Africa, societies had mastered C-sections and discovered inoculation against deadly diseases. Advanced states, such as the Regency of Algeria, the Kingdom of Zimbabwe, and the Empire of Mali existed, and different African civilizations created stunning cities, such as the Great Zimbabwe, Timbuktu, and Kilwa Kisiwani. In Ghana, real wages remained higher than in almost all of Northern Europe before colonialism. When the Europeans arrived and began the process of colonization, many of these advancements were destroyed. See, Africa has always been a rich continent- rich in both hardworking inhabitants and in natural resources. Africa’s labor force was stolen by European slavery (a process abetted by some greedy African tribal leaders) and many of Africa’s natural resources were stolen through colonialism. As a result, life expectancy, average height, and overall standards of living plummeted. When improvements in the quality of life for ordinary Africans occurred, they happened despite colonialism, not because of it. These improvements also largely happened during the 20th century, when anti-colonial movements were gathering steam. But the legacy of colonialism remains difficult to overcome (in part because colonialism never ended). In many parts of Africa, real wages and human stature have yet to recover from colonialism began[1]. In conclusion, colonialism drastically hurt Africa. It’s impossible to know what Africa would be like without Africa. But we can say for certain that colonialism hurt Africa, and it has only been thanks to the struggles of anti-colonial movements that some parts of Africa have recovered. Stay safe, -Ben *I also want to note that Africa is a massive and diverse continent, and colonialism impacted different parts in very different ways. However, overall, it has been scientifically proven that colonialism caused a downturn in living standards for ordinary Africans.

So, these are the top 10 most powerful mortal force users in Legends. Question: How do you pass the rancor in Star Wars: KOTOR?
Answer: Well, Aspyr is remaking Knights of the Old Republic so I figured I’d do a couple KotOR themed answers. Anyway, the first thing you need to do to pass the Rancor is to get the synthesized odor from the severed arm right outside the Rancor’s lair. Getting this is critical to defeating the rancor. Then, switch over to Mission. (I like to use her since she’s the best at stealth). Click the stealth button in the bottom left to turn on the stealth field generator. Then, as Mission and concealed by the stealth field generator, walk over to the corpse pile in the middle of the Rancor’s room. Switch to “give items,” and place the synthesized odor and any grenades you found earlier in the corpse pile. After that, a cutscene will play in which the Rancor will run over the corpse pile. The Rancor will eat the corpse pile and all the grenades it in. The Rancor will explode, allowing you to pass to the next room unopposed. So, that is how you pass the Rancor in Knights of the Old Republic. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: Who/What was Yuuzhan Vong?
Answer: Alright, so this will basically be a short crash course on the Vong for anyone wanting to learn about them. The Vong were a nihilistic alien race from outside the Star Wars Galaxy. After their own galaxy was devastated by wars, the Vong left their galaxy and traveled through the intergalactic void to the Star Wars Galaxy. After sending in various probes and spies, they invaded the galaxy in 25 ABY. The Vong were a warrior culture, and used completely organic technology. Everything, from their starships to battlecruisers to melee weapons, were living beings. The Vong (partly because of a devastating war between to droid races in their galaxy) were extremely technophobic. The Yuuzhan Vong traveled in massive living worldships, the largest of which, the Banuu Rass, was over 100km in length. At the end of each arm you can see a Miid Ro’ik class cruiser, a photo of which I’ll post in the comments. This can give you a good sense of how massive the things are. The Vong were very religious. They worshipped various gods, such as Yun-Yuuzhan (the creator) and Yun-Harla, the trickster god. The Vong would often make sacrifices to these gods, and even the idea that these gods might not exist was blashpemy. The Vong also had a very strict caste system. The Shamed Ones were at the bottom, and the Shaper and Warrior Castes at the top. The Shaper Caste not only helped grow the Vong’s living weapons, but also did body modifications, something the Vong were extremely fond of. So, that is what you need to know about the Yuuzhan Vong in Legends. In fact, the Yuuzhan Vong caused 365 trillion deaths and permanently messed up Jaina and Jacen Solo. I could go on an on about the Vong- about how they had a living planet called Zenoma Sekot and they had a torture device called the embrace of pain- but that’s ofr another day. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: In Star Wars: Episode II, Obi-Wan says, "If droids could think, there'd be none of us here." What do you think he means by that?
Answer: This is actually a really clever bit of foreshadowing. This line foreshadows General Grievous and Darth Vader. Both are cyborgs, and have droid parts- but they have independent thought. And both are extremely prolific Jedi killers- Grievous has many lightsabers in his collection, and Vader has killed many Jedi. See, the clone wars pits droids against clones. The droids are fairly stupid and aren’t very smart- we see their incompetence displayed multiple times in the trilogy. Their opponents, clones, however, are living, human beings, who can think. So what Obi-Wan is really saying is that if they fight a living opponent that could think independently and could be deployed in large numbers, they would wipe out the Jedi. And, one movie later, that is exactly what happens. So, in conclusion, when Obi-Wan said "If droids could think, there'd be none of us here,” he was foreshadowing Vader, Grievous, and Order 66. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: In Star Wars, was the Empire truly imperial? Did it expand the star systems under Republic protection to include Separatist and neutral systems?
Answer: Yes. In Legends, in the days of the Republic, many systems in the Outer and Mid Rim completely ignored Republic authority, paying at most lip service to the government on Coruscant. Most of these planets expected the Empire to pay them as little heed as the Republic did. To quote the Essential Guide to Warfare, [Following the Clone Wars] many Rim words remained lawless, paying the newborn Empire as little mind as they had the Republic. Things were about to change. The Empire continued to accelerate ship and vehicle production, and used these forces to establish a permanent presence on many Outer Rim worlds. The Empire also ruthlessly pursued Separatist holdouts, using the presence of Trade Federation and Sy Myrthian loyalists to justify heavy-handed military occupations of distant planets. The presence of Sy Myrthian separatist holdouts even gave the Empire an excuse to annex a swath of Hutt Space. The Empire ruthlessly exploited these newly-conquered planets. Slavery was nationalized, and entire species, such as the Wookiees, were deemed completely expendable. Renowned Imperial admirals were gifted planets to be run as slave plantations. Meanwhile, the Empire allowed corporations to dominate tens of thousands of planets in the Outer Rim. In conclusion, between the forceful seizure of territory, nationalized slavery, and corporate domination, the Empire was certainly an Empire. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: What's the worst war crime that no one knows about?
Answer: The sanctioning of Iraq from 1991–2003. In 1991, the United States (US) fought Iraq after Iraq had invaded Kuwait* in what became known as the First Gulf War. The US routed Iraqi troops and liberated oil-rich Kuwait. During the conflict, the US dropped massive amounts of bombs on Iraq, relegating Iraq to a “pre-industrial age[1],”, according to the United Nations (UN). The US then withdrew from Iraq, allowing Saddam Hussein, the Iraqi dictator, to remain in power. However, although the US did withdraw it’s troops from Iraq, it did not leave the country alone. The US and the United Kingdom imposed numerous no-fly zones and sanctions on Iraq. The sanctions in particular were devastating towards Iraq’s economy. Without their ability to rebuild civilian infrastructure, millions of Iraqis went without food or water, and the Iraqi healthcare system was devastated[2]. The Iraqi sanctions were aimed to make the Iraqi population hungry, which the US hoped would force them rebel against Saddam Hussein. However, the opposite happened. Although millions of Iraqis starved, the sanctions forced them to depend more on Saddam Hussein, and furthered the reach of his dictatorship. The human cost of the Iraq sanctions are difficult to quantify, but they are massive. By 1995, the UN[3] was reporting that 500,000 Iraqi children had been killed by the sanctions. Many more likely died in the next 8 years, not to mention the millions that were forced to go without food or shelter. Of course, this humanitarian catastrophe hardly seemed to affect American leadership. In 1996, when asked about whether the deaths of 500,000 Iraqi children were worth it[4], then-Secretary of State Madeline Albright replied with a resounding “yes.” The sanctions would only be brought to an end by the Iraq War, when the US, after falsely claiming Iraq possessed WMDs, invaded Iraq. This invasion sparked a decades-long civil war and the flaring up of Sunni-Shia relations, the consequences of which are still being felt today. Sincerely, -Ben *It should be noted that Iraq, prior to the invasion of Kuwait, Iraq had been heavily backed by the United States. It’s even possible that the invasion of Kuwait had been caused by Hussein misinterpreting American orders[5]. It’s also important to note that Hussein offered to withdraw his troops several times from Kuwait before the US invasion. ** I also want to clarify that while Hussein was an awful person, that hardly justifies the sanctions, which hurt Iraqi people and strengthen Hussein’s dictatorship. The average Iraqi was not involved in Al-Anfal and didn’t use chemical weapons in Iran.

Question: What are the most military like books in the star wars world?
Answer: There are several good war novels that I love in Star Wars. In Legends, we have multiple books like this. One of my personal favorites is X-Wing: Rogue Squadron, which is basically top-gun in space. We get introduced to some fan-favorite characters like Corran Horn, and see some other characters like Wedge Antilles and Tycho Celuchu. Another book I love is Rebel Dream, the first book in the Enemy Lines Duology. (The second book, Rebel Stand, is great as well, but it is less of a war novel). Anyway, this book covers the Battle of Borelias and the fallout from the f all of Coruscant. Not only is it well written, but the way they cover the dynamic in the New Republic after the fall of Coruscant is handled quite well. There are other such books that would fall into this category as well that I have varying degrees of fondness for. I do enjoy Darksaber, Shadows of Mindor is fine, and I dislike Republic Commadno. However, the ultimate “military book” is the Essential Guide to Warfare. This is one of my favorite Star Wars books, and I have read it at least a dozen times. I would highly recommend it. In canon, the only one that comes to mind is the Battlefront (2015) book. I really enjoyed it actually, being one of the few good (or even passable) canon books out there. It covers the 61st Mobile Infantry company and is a pretty harsh, yet enthralling, read. It really made me nostalgic for the Rebel Alliance Sourcebook while reading it. So, those are the most military like books in Star Wars. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: How is there gravity on Star Wars ships?
Answer: Ships have artificial gravity. We see this in canon in the Rebels episode Spark of Rebellion. In the episode, Sabine turns off the artificial gravity in the ship, causing everyone to start floating around, allowing the Rebels to escape. Question: Did Darth Vader have any friends?
Answer: He had one. Following the Battle of Hoth, the Galactic Empire created a massive battlestation above the planet Hockaleg. Rebel infiltrators attacked and destroyed the station, before fleeing in the Millenium Falcon, with Darth Vader pursuing in his TIE Fighter. However, Luke Skywalker dumped the Falcon’s water supply, turning it into ice and damaging Vader’s ship, leaving him stranded in space. Vader was rescued by a stormtrooper. Upon questioning the trooper, Vader learned that the trooper was an old clone, CT-4981. He had served under Anakin Skywalker during the Clone Wars, flying as Shadow Eleven under Skywalker at Kadavo and the Kaliida Nebula. Vader then learned that the trooper had been demoted after disobeying an order to kill a friend. Upon questioning the trooper, Vader learned that CT-4981- nicknamed Contrail- would disobey orders if it prolonged Vader’s life- an act that stunned and moved Vader. When Vader and Contrail returned to Hockaleg, they were ambushed by rebel dockworkers. Several of the dock workers managed to attack Vader while his back was turned- however, Contrail dived in front of the blaster fire, sacrificing himself to save the Dark Lord. As Contrail lay dying, in an act that mirrored Vader’s later death on the Second Death Star, the Sith Lord removed Contrail’s helmet to find the aged face of a clone of Jango Fett staring up at him. Vader revealed that he was Anakin Skywalker, and Contrail did not seem surprised as he died. In conclusion, in Legends, Vader did have a friend, the clone trooper Contrail. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: How did Gilead Paelleon die?
Answer: He was assassinated during the Battle of Fondor. See, the Galactic Alliance, lead by Jacen Solo and Cha Niathal (the two were Joint Chiefs of State) were at war with the Confederation in the year 41 ABY. Though the Alliance had seen success, and the tide was currently, in their favor, the Alliance’s advance was slow and their forces spread thin across the galaxy. Solo decided that a way to achieve a breakthrough victory would be to take out the planet Fondor. Fondor was the Confederation’s largest shipyard, and had been producing ships for the war effort nonstop since the fighting had begun a year ago. However, in order to get enough ships for the large push on Fondor, the Alliance needed the support of the Imperial Remnant, lead by Gilead Paelleon and the Moff Council. Pressured by the Moff Council, Paelleon agreed that the Imperial Remnant would help take Fondor- in exchange for Borelias and Bilbringi, two planets known for their banking and shipbuilding, respectively. However, wary of Solo, Paelleon called for an old friend who owed him an important debt- Natasi Daala, who had gone missing and was presumed dead 23 years earlier during the Battle of Champala. The Galactic Alliance and Imperial Remnant forces attacked Fondor and , despite initial setbacks, saw great success, smashing through the Confederation defenses and establishing aerial dominance over the planet. In order to force Fondor to surrender, Solo, (now a Sith Lord) began firing on the civilian centers of Fondor. Even after the Fondorians surrendered, Solo continued his bombardment, killing millions. Disgusted, Niathal turned on Jacen and ordered all Galactic Alliance forces to attack him. However, two thirds of the GA forces sided with Solo. Jacen’s Sith apprentice, Tahiri Veila, was sent to Paelleon’s flagship, the Bloodfin, to demand that Paelleon assist Jacen. Paelleon refused, and Veila threatened him with death if he failed to comply. When Paelleon did not listen to Veila and ordered the Remnant to join Niathal, Veila executed Paelleon. Paelleon’s choice to side with Niathal, even though he knew it would cost him his life, is the conclusion of Paelleon’s multi-book story arc. In 8 ABY, Paelleon had joined Thrawn during his campaign, and later joined a reborn Darth Sidious during Operation Shadow Hand. Paelleon wished to bring about the Empire he viewed had gone up in flames with the Second Darth Star- one that emphasized loyalty and order, yet was just and fair. Paelleon watched the Crimson Empire rise and fall, joining Treutan Teradoc, the largest of the Warlords in the Deep Core. However, Teradoc and the other warlords were worse than the Imperials he had left behind, wasting their soldiers in fruitless battles among the densest-packed stars in the galaxy. Paelleon found hope in Natasi Daala, who lured the Deep Core warlords to Tsoss Beacon before executing the lot of them. However, as Daala wasted her opportunity on a failed attack on the Jedi Praxeum at Yavin IV, Paelleon realized the Empire he had remembered had never existed. Taking command of the remnants of the Crimson Empire and whatever Daala had left behind, Paelleon formed the Imperial Remnant, making peace with the New Republic and making the Empire what he always dreamed of- an orderly, secure, and peaceful state- though an admittedly undemocratic one. At Fondor, however, we see Paelleon truly cement his status as a hero. Paelleon was torn between siding with Jacen Solo- who’s Palpatinian actions symbolized the Empire- and the Mon Calamari Cha Niathal, who represented the New Republic. As Paelleon lay dying and ordered his forces to join Niathal, Palleon finally embraced democracy and the light. Cha Niathal Paelleon’s sacrifice was not in vain. Though the Moffs’ disobeyed Paelleon and joined Solo, Daala, continuing Paelleon’s legacy, arrived with a large armada. Her forces were able to temporarily drive of Solo. Niathal and the Fondorian government formed the Alliance-in-exile, with help from the Jedi Coalition, leaving Jacen Solo- a Sith Lord- in complete control of the Galactic Alliance. Sp, that is the story behind Paelleon’s death at the Battle of Fondor. Stay safe, -Ben

Question: What's stopping Palpatine from returning after The Rise of Skywalker?

In Dark Empire, Palpatine returns from the grave in clone bodies and leads a massive, superweapon filled assault on the galaxy. Question: What would have been a better plot for the Star Wars Sequel Trilogy?
Answer: What they’re starting to flesh out in the new canon books. While I’ve complained a lot about the world-building in the Star Wars sequels, I think in some ways their setting is quite interesting. A fascist Imperial rump state slowly building up arms while the New Republic is divided by bickering, forcing our heroes to take up underground armed resistance is a fascinating premise. It would also play off of the prequel trilogy in a fun way, as our heroes, rather than unconditionally serving a failed Republic, have realized that working outside of the system is the only way to affect change. Seeing this intergalactic confrontation play out would add some much-needed substance to The Force Awakens, help explain Luke’s absence, and would help differentiate the movie from A New Hope. A scene where the New Republic senate condemns Resistance leaders for engaging First Order troops on Takodana, while simultaneously failing to call out the First Order for invading the planet in the first place, would also help explain why Leia and Admiral Ackbar founded the resistance in the first place. These stories were glaring absent from the movies (the most accessible form of Star Wars content), and it’s very frustating that such a great storytelling opportunity was simply ignored. Hopefully though, these stories will be told in the new canon via books and comics as it begins to find its footing. Stay safe, -Ben
